objectives: Trace viral life cycles from lytic to lysogenic to retroviral.
Map major human viruses + phage therapy revival.

slides.title: Viral structure + Baltimore classification — life on the edge of life
slides.body:
**Viruses** are obligate intracellular acellular replicators: nucleic acid (DNA or RNA, single- or double-stranded) + a protein capsid, sometimes a lipid envelope, often nothing else. They lack ribosomes, ATP-generation, biosynthesis — they hijack host cells for everything. Whether viruses are 'alive' is a definitional question; their evolutionary impact is undisputed.

**Discovery**: **Beijerinck (1898)** filtered tobacco-mosaic-disease sap through bacterial-trapping filters; the still-infectious filtrate revealed an entity smaller than any bacterium. Beijerinck named it **contagium vivum fluidum** ('contagious living fluid') — the first virus. Independently of Ivanovsky (1892). The word 'virus' (Latin: poison) was generalized.

**Numerical importance**: ~10³¹ virus particles on Earth (~10× more than cells); ~10⁹ phages per mL of seawater; kill ~20-40% of marine bacteria daily; massive effect on global carbon + nutrient cycling (viral shunt). Foundational work by **Bratbak, Fuhrman, Suttle, Sullivan, Rohwer**.

**Capsid architecture** — protein shells encoding the genome:
- **Icosahedral**: 20-faced regular polyhedron from 60 (or T × 60) protein subunits via triangulation number T (Caspar-Klug 1962). Examples: polio, adenovirus, HSV, T7, SV40.
- **Helical**: protein subunits arranged in a helix around the nucleic acid. Examples: tobacco mosaic virus (TMV — first solved, Klug Nobel 1982), influenza nucleocapsids, rabies.
- **Complex**: tailed bacteriophages (T4, λ — icosahedral head + helical tail + baseplate + tail fibers).
- **Pleomorphic**: enveloped viruses with no single shape (HIV, influenza).

**Envelope**: lipid bilayer **from host membrane** acquired during budding, embedded with viral glycoproteins. Enveloped viruses (influenza, HIV, coronaviruses, herpes, hepatitis B, Ebola) are typically sensitive to soap + alcohol (membrane disrupted). Non-enveloped viruses (polio, hepatitis A, norovirus, adenovirus, HPV) are more environmentally stable — relevant to fomite + waterborne transmission.

**Baltimore classification** (David Baltimore 1971; Nobel 1975 for reverse-transcriptase discovery 1970 along with Howard Temin + Renato Dulbecco) — based on **how genome → mRNA**, the unifying problem every virus must solve:

- **I. dsDNA**: HSV, VZV, EBV, HPV, adenovirus, poxvirus, phages T4 + λ. Most use host RNA polymerase; some encode their own.
- **II. ssDNA**: parvovirus B19, AAV (gene-therapy vector), φX174 phage (first sequenced genome — Sanger 1977).
- **III. dsRNA**: rotavirus (major childhood diarrhea), reovirus. Packaged RNA polymerase makes mRNA from genome.
- **IV. (+)ssRNA**: poliovirus, hepatitis A, hepatitis C, HCV, Zika, dengue, yellow fever, west Nile, SARS-CoV-2, all coronaviruses, rhinoviruses, enteroviruses, tobacco mosaic virus. Genome directly serves as mRNA upon entry — fastest from arrival to protein synthesis.
- **V. (−)ssRNA**: influenza (segmented), measles, mumps, rabies, RSV, parainfluenza, hantavirus, Ebola + Marburg (filoviruses), Lassa. Packaged RdRp transcribes (−)genome → (+)mRNA.
- **VI. RNA reverse-transcribing**: HIV-1 + HIV-2, HTLV-1, all retroviruses. ssRNA genome + reverse transcriptase + integrase → integrated proviral DNA in host genome. Endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) compose ~8% of the human genome — fossils of ancient retroviral infections.
- **VII. DNA reverse-transcribing**: hepatitis B (HBV), cauliflower mosaic virus (plants). Replicate via an RNA intermediate + reverse transcriptase.

**Genome sizes**: HIV ~9.7 kb (9 proteins); influenza 8 segments totaling ~13 kb; coronavirus ~30 kb (largest ssRNA); poxvirus ~200 kb; herpesvirus ~150-230 kb; **giant viruses** — Mimivirus (~1.2 Mb, 1000 genes; discovered in *Acanthamoeba* 2003 by **La Scola + Raoult**; larger than many bacteria), Pandoravirus (~2.5 Mb), Pithovirus, Megavirus. Force reconsideration of what 'virus' means. Some giant viruses encode translation-machinery components, blurring viral-cellular boundaries.

**Phages**: viruses of bacteria + archaea. Most abundant biological entities. Tailed phages of the Caudoviricetes (T4, λ, P22, T7, Mu, etc.) dominate. Foundation of molecular biology: lambda integration → Campbell model; T4 genetics → Benzer fine structure; phage display (Smith Nobel 2018); CRISPR-Cas (phage-defense origin); huge bacteriophage discovery in metagenomics (Banfield lab huge phages, jumbo phages, megaphages).

slides.title: Viral life cycles — lytic, lysogenic, latent, persistent + retroviral
slides.body:
Every viral replication cycle solves the same six problems: **attachment, entry, uncoating, replication + transcription, assembly, release**.

**1. Attachment**: viral surface protein binds host receptor:
- Influenza HA → sialic acid.
- HIV gp120 → CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptor.
- SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) → ACE2 (TMPRSS2 protease cleaves spike).
- Rabies G → nicotinic ACh receptor + others.
- Adenovirus fiber knob → CAR.
- Receptor specificity sets **tropism + host range**.

**2. Entry + uncoating**: routes:
- **Direct fusion at the plasma membrane** (HIV, paramyxoviruses) — fusion protein conformational change.
- **Receptor-mediated endocytosis** + endosomal fusion (influenza HA refolds at acidic pH; M2 ion channel acidifies interior).
- **Membrane translocation** (some non-enveloped).
- **Phage injection**: tail contraction delivers genome through cell wall + membrane; capsid stays outside.

**3. Replication + transcription**: location + strategy depends on Baltimore class:
- Most DNA viruses replicate in the **nucleus**, using host RNA polymerase + DNA polymerase (or viral). Exception: **poxviruses** replicate entirely in cytoplasm with their own machinery.
- Most RNA viruses replicate in **cytoplasm** (exception: influenza + retroviruses use nucleus).
- (+)ssRNA: translation from genome → polyprotein → viral protease cleaves → including RdRp → makes (−)template → makes more (+) for new genomes + mRNA.
- (−)ssRNA: virion-packaged RdRp transcribes (−) → (+)mRNA → genome replication.
- Retroviruses: virion-packaged **reverse transcriptase** (Baltimore + Temin 1970) → dsDNA → integrase inserts into host genome → proviral DNA transcribed by host machinery.

**4. Assembly**: capsid + genome assemble (self-assembly, often with scaffold proteins + ATPase packaging motors for dsDNA viruses).

**5. Release**:
- **Lysis** — disrupt the host cell (most non-enveloped + phages; endolysin + holin in phages).
- **Budding** — enveloped viruses acquire lipid envelope while exiting (HIV, influenza, coronaviruses, herpes — at PM, ER, Golgi, or nuclear envelope depending on virus).
- **Cell-to-cell spread** — viral synapses (HIV), syncytia formation (RSV, measles).

**Lytic vs lysogenic — phage lambda (λ) decision** (one of the great molecular biology stories; **Allan Campbell, François Jacob, Mark Ptashne, Susan Gottesman**):
- After infection, λ commits to either **lytic** (replicate + lyse + release ~100 phages per cell in ~30 min) or **lysogenic** (integrate into host chromosome as **prophage**, replicate silently as part of host genome, indefinitely; can later excise + re-enter lytic — **induction** by DNA damage via RecA + SOS response).
- The lysis/lysogeny **switch** is the classic genetic toggle (cI repressor + cII activator + Cro repressor; mutual antagonism; bistable). Foundational regulatory-circuit example.
- Prophages may carry virulence genes — **lysogenic conversion**: Shiga toxin in *E. coli* O157:H7 (Stx phage), diphtheria toxin (CTφ-like in Corynebacterium), cholera toxin (CTXφ in V. cholerae). Mekalanos showed that many key bacterial virulence factors are encoded on prophages.

**Latency in animal viruses**:
- **Herpesviruses**: lifelong latency in neurons (HSV in trigeminal/sacral ganglia, VZV in dorsal root ganglia → reactivation as shingles); LCL in B cells (EBV). Periodic reactivation.
- **HIV**: latent provirus in resting memory CD4⁺ T cells — the reservoir that prevents cure with current therapy.
- **Hepatitis B**: cccDNA persists in hepatocyte nuclei — also a cure barrier.

**Persistent infection** without latency: HCV (lifelong replication in some), HIV in untreated, chronic HBV.

**Reverse transcription + the retroviral cycle (Baltimore + Temin 1970, Nobel 1975)**:
- Two ssRNA copies + reverse transcriptase + integrase + protease packaged per virion.
- After entry, RT copies RNA → dsDNA in cytoplasm.
- Integrase delivers dsDNA into nucleus + inserts at random into host genome → **provirus**.
- Provirus transcribed by host machinery → genomic + spliced mRNAs → Gag, Pol, Env polyproteins → cleaved by viral protease (HIV PR → target of saquinavir + lopinavir + darunavir + many).
- Budding at PM → maturation outside.
- **AZT** (1987 first HIV antiretroviral) inhibits RT; **protease inhibitors** (1995) revolutionized HIV treatment; **integrase inhibitors** (raltegravir, dolutegravir, bictegravir) + entry/fusion inhibitors complete modern **HAART/cART** combinations.

**Influenza segmentation** — the basis of pandemics:
- 8 (−)ssRNA segments encoding 10-14 proteins.
- **Antigenic drift**: gradual mutation of HA + NA each season → seasonal influenza, annual vaccine updates.
- **Antigenic shift**: reassortment of segments between strains co-infecting one cell → novel HA/NA → no population immunity → **pandemic**. 1918 H1N1 'Spanish flu' (~50M deaths; **Taubenberger** sequenced from preserved tissue, 1997+); 1957 H2N2, 1968 H3N2, 1977 H1N1, 2009 H1N1 'swine flu'. Avian H5N1 + H7N9 + H5N8 are ongoing pandemic-risk lineages (Fouchier + Kawaoka gain-of-function experiments, 2011-12, sparked dual-use research debate).

slides.title: Major human viruses + phage therapy
slides.body:
**HIV (1981 AIDS recognized; 1983 virus isolated)**:
- Identified independently by **Françoise Barré-Sinoussi + Luc Montagnier** (Institut Pasteur, 1983) + by **Robert Gallo** (NCI, 1984). Priority dispute resolved by 2002 settlement; Montagnier + Barré-Sinoussi shared 2008 Nobel.
- Lentivirus (Retroviridae). Targets CD4⁺ T cells via CD4 + CCR5/CXCR4. Progressive immune destruction → opportunistic infections (PCP, KS, TB, CMV, candidiasis, MAC) + AIDS-defining illnesses.
- ~38 million people living with HIV (2024); ~1.3 million new infections + ~630000 deaths annually. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) → near-normal life expectancy; U=U (undetectable = untransmittable). Long-acting injectables (cabotegravir + rilpivirine) + PrEP + PEP transform prevention.
- **Cure attempts**: Berlin patient (Brown 2007, allogeneic CCR5-Δ32 stem-cell transplant); London + Düsseldorf + New York patients (similar mechanism). Reservoir + cccDNA = barriers. CRISPR + shock-and-kill + block-and-lock strategies under investigation.

**Influenza**:
- A, B, C (D in cattle). Influenza A subtypes by HA (1-18) + NA (1-11). Major human subtypes H1N1, H3N2, plus influenza B Yamagata + Victoria.
- Seasonal vaccine reformulated yearly (WHO selects strains based on surveillance); ~40-60% efficacy in good years.
- **Universal flu vaccine** — long-sought; targets conserved HA stem (Nabel, Wilson, Nussenzweig). bNAb-eliciting immunogens; mRNA platforms (Moderna mRNA-1010).
- **Oseltamivir + zanamivir + baloxavir** for treatment.

**Hepatitis B + C**:
- HBV — dsDNA partial; chronic infection → cirrhosis + HCC. ~300M chronic globally. Vaccine (Blumberg Nobel 1976 for HBsAg discovery → recombinant vaccine 1986) — first cancer vaccine. Cure via cccDNA elimination still elusive.
- HCV — (+)ssRNA Flaviviridae. ~70M chronic. **Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)** revolutionized care: sofosbuvir (NS5B polymerase inhibitor; Gilead 2013), ledipasvir + velpatasvir (NS5A), grazoprevir (NS3 protease). 95+% cure rates in 8-12 weeks of oral therapy — among the great therapeutic successes of the 21st century. **Houghton + Rice + Alter** Nobel Medicine 2020 for HCV discovery + replication.

**Herpesviruses** (Herpesviridae) — 8 human:
- HSV-1, HSV-2 (cold sores, genital herpes; lifelong latency in neurons).
- VZV (chickenpox + shingles; vaccines Varivax + Shingrix).
- EBV (mononucleosis; Burkitt + nasopharyngeal carcinoma; multiple sclerosis association proven 2022 Ascherio).
- CMV (TORCH congenital infection; transplant + AIDS).
- HHV-6, HHV-7, KSHV/HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma + PEL + Castleman disease — Chang + Moore discovery 1994).

**HPV** (Human papillomavirus):
- dsDNA non-enveloped. >200 types. High-risk types (16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) cause ~5% of all cancers worldwide: cervical, anal, oropharyngeal, penile, vulvar, vaginal.
- **Harald zur Hausen** Nobel 2008 — established HPV-cervical cancer causation despite decades of skepticism.
- Gardasil + Cervarix vaccines (recombinant L1 VLPs) — among the most successful cancer-preventive interventions. Australia + UK on track to eliminate cervical cancer.

**Ebola + Marburg** (Filoviridae, (−)ssRNA):
- Highly virulent (case-fatality ~25-90%). Sporadic outbreaks in central + west Africa; 2014-16 West African outbreak killed ~11000. Reservoir likely fruit bats.
- **Ervebo (rVSV-ZEBOV)** vaccine (Merck, approved 2019) + monoclonal antibody therapies (Inmazeb, Ebanga).

**Coronaviruses**:
- (+)ssRNA, ~30 kb largest RNA genome. 7 human coronaviruses: 4 common-cold (HCoV-229E, OC43, NL63, HKU1) + 3 severe (**SARS-CoV** 2002-03 Hong Kong-China-global, ~10% CFR, ~800 deaths; **MERS-CoV** 2012- Saudi Arabia + camels, ~35% CFR; **SARS-CoV-2** 2019- pandemic, ~7M reported deaths + likely >20M total).
- COVID-19 response showcased vaccine + therapeutics platforms: **mRNA vaccines** (Karikó + Weissman Nobel Medicine 2023; Pfizer-BioNTech BNT162b2; Moderna mRNA-1273), adenovirus-vector (AstraZeneca, J&J, Sputnik V), inactivated (Sinovac, Sinopharm); **monoclonal antibodies** (REGEN-COV, sotrovimab, bebtelovimab); **Paxlovid** (nirmatrelvir + ritonavir, oral protease inhibitor); **molnupiravir** (lethal mutagenesis). Sequencing-driven surveillance (Nextstrain, GISAID).

**Zika**: (+)ssRNA Flavivirus. 2015-16 Americas outbreak revealed congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly + brain malformations from in-utero infection. Sexual + vector (*Aedes*) transmission. Vaccines in development.

**Phage therapy** — using bacteriophages as antibacterial agents:
- **Felix d'Hérelle** (Pasteur Institute, 1917) — co-discovered phages (with Twort 1915); coined 'bacteriophage' + immediately proposed therapeutic use; treated dysentery + cholera in patients (Paris + India 1920s).
- **Eliava Institute** (Tbilisi, Georgia, 1923-) — d'Hérelle's collaborator George Eliava founded the institute that maintained phage therapy through the Soviet era + remains a global reference today.
- Largely abandoned in the West after penicillin (1940s) due to inconsistent results + lack of standardization.
- **Modern revival** driven by multidrug-resistance (AMR) crisis + improved phage isolation, characterization, GMP production. Notable case: **Tom Patterson 2016** (UCSD) — first US documented life-saving compassionate-use phage therapy for MDR *Acinetobacter baumannii* (Strathdee + Schooley + Hatfull). 
- **Adaptive Phage Therapeutics, BiomX, Locus Biosciences, Armata Pharmaceuticals, Pherecydes** + others now pursue clinical phage products; multiple ongoing trials.
- **Engineered phages**: CRISPR-armed phages (Locus), synthetic phages, phage cocktails. **Graham Hatfull** + Howard Hughes/Pittsburgh phage hunters discovered + characterized thousands of mycobacteriophages; provided personalized phage cocktail for a CF patient with disseminated MDR *Mycobacterium abscessus* (2019, *Nature Medicine*).
- Combined with antibiotics (synergy + resistance reversal — Levin), phage therapy may become a key AMR-era adjunct.

question.question: Trace a (+)ssRNA virus from entry to release
question.goal: Step through the SARS-CoV-2 life cycle + identify key intervention points (existing + potential drugs).

steps.prompt: Attachment + entry of SARS-CoV-2 — what's the receptor + protease?

acceptedAnswers: Spike → ACE2; TMPRSS2 cleaves; or endosomal entry via cathepsins

steps.reveal: Spike (S) binds ACE2 on respiratory epithelium. **TMPRSS2** cleaves S → conformational change → membrane fusion at PM. Alternative endosomal route uses cathepsin B/L. Spike has two subunits (S1 binding + S2 fusion). **Neutralizing antibodies** (vaccine, mAb therapy) target spike RBD. Camostat + nafamostat (TMPRSS2 inhibitors) failed in trials.

steps.prompt: Translation + replication — what does the (+)ssRNA genome do first?

acceptedAnswers: Translated directly → polyprotein → 3CLpro/PLpro process → including RdRp

steps.reveal: (+)ssRNA acts as mRNA immediately — ribosomes translate ORF1a + ORF1ab (via -1 frameshift) → pp1a + pp1ab polyproteins → cleaved by **3CLpro (main protease, Mpro) + PLpro** into 16 nonstructural proteins including **RdRp (nsp12)**, helicase, exonuclease (nsp14 proofreading — unique among RNA viruses). RdRp synthesizes (−) template + new (+) genomes + sgRNAs.

steps.prompt: Where do drugs hit? Remdesivir, molnupiravir, nirmatrelvir.
steps.reveal: **Remdesivir** (Gilead) — nucleotide analog incorporated by RdRp → delayed chain termination. **Molnupiravir** (Merck) — lethal mutagenesis (N-hydroxycytidine → C-U or C-A misincorporation). **Nirmatrelvir / Paxlovid** (Pfizer) — covalent peptidomimetic 3CLpro inhibitor; given with ritonavir CYP3A4 booster. Each ~50-90% efficacy at reducing severe outcomes if started <5 days from symptom onset.

acceptedAnswers: Assembly at ERGIC; budding into ER-Golgi; release by exocytosis

steps.reveal: Coronaviruses assemble at the **ERGIC (ER-Golgi intermediate compartment)**: N protein + genome + M, E + S accessories. Bud into ER-Golgi lumen → trafficked through Golgi → released by exocytosis (not classical PM budding). E protein viroporin role; spike processed by furin (S1/S2 cleavage during transit) + later by TMPRSS2 (S2′ cleavage at next-cell entry). Targets for future drugs: furin inhibitors, viroporin blockers.

steps.prompt: What does proofreading by nsp14 imply for resistance?

acceptedAnswers: Lower mutation rate than most RNA viruses; slower resistance evolution + larger genome possible

steps.reveal: Coronaviruses uniquely encode **nsp14 ExoN proofreader** → ~10× lower mutation rate than other RNA viruses. Allows ~30 kb genome (other RNA viruses max ~15 kb). Means slower drug-resistance evolution + slower antigenic drift relative to influenza — but evolution still happens (Alpha → Delta → Omicron → KP.3 → JN.1 → ...). Combinations of antivirals + vaccine-driven immunity slow resistance further.

question.question: Why was Baltimore + Temin's 1970 discovery of reverse transcriptase a paradigm shift?
options: **Reverse transcriptase** (Baltimore 1970 *Nature*; Temin 1970 *Nature*; Nobel 1975 with Dulbecco) — an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase — directly violated the **central dogma**'s assumed unidirectional flow (DNA → RNA → protein). It established that **RNA viruses (retroviruses)** maintain their genome by copying RNA → DNA + integrating into host chromosomes. This: (1) explained tumor virology (Rous sarcoma virus + later HTLV-1 + HIV); (2) introduced **provirus + integration** + the concept of endogenous retroviruses (now known to be ~8% of human genome — fossils of past infections); (3) gave molecular biology its single most important enzyme tool — **RT** is the basis of **cDNA cloning** (Verma 1972), RNA-seq, qRT-PCR, single-cell RNA-seq, RT-PCR diagnostics (COVID, HIV viral load); (4) enabled HIV antiretroviral therapy (AZT 1987 + countless successors targeting RT); (5) reframed the central dogma to allow reverse + lateral information flow. A textbook + tool-revolutionizing discovery.
question.explanation: Baltimore + Temin (1970 Nature; Nobel 1975) discovered reverse transcriptase — RNA-dependent DNA polymerase — violating the assumed unidirectional central dogma. Established retrovirus + provirus biology; introduced ERVs (~8% human genome); revolutionized molecular biology tools (cDNA cloning, RT-PCR, RNA-seq, scRNA-seq); enabled HIV antiretroviral therapy. Textbook + tool-revolutionizing.

slides.workedSolution: Reverse transcriptase (Baltimore + Temin 1970 Nature; Nobel 1975) violated central-dogma unidirectionality. Established retrovirus + integration + provirus biology + ERV concept. Tool revolution: cDNA cloning, RT-PCR, RNA-seq, scRNA-seq. Enabled HIV antiretroviral therapy. Textbook + tool revolutionizing.

question.question: Phage therapy for MDR Acinetobacter
question.prompt: A patient has a multidrug-resistant *Acinetobacter baumannii* infection unresponsive to all antibiotics (the Tom Patterson 2016 scenario). Design a phage-therapy plan: (1) sourcing + screening phages (banks, environmental sampling, Eliava); (2) lytic vs temperate selection + why; (3) cocktail design + characterization (host range, kinetics, endotoxin, regulatory); (4) administration route + monitoring; (5) combining with antibiotics (synergy with colistin? phage steering toward resistance reversal?); (6) regulatory pathway (compassionate use, expanded access, phase trials). Reference d'Hérelle 1917 + Strathdee + Schooley + Hatfull.

question.question: Roughly how many virus particles are estimated to exist on Earth (order of magnitude)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, summarize what a virus is + why virology drives modern medicine + biology.
question.rubric: Mentions: viruses = obligate intracellular acellular replicators; nucleic-acid + capsid ± envelope; ~10³¹ particles globally, ~10× cells. Discovery Beijerinck 1898 contagium vivum fluidum. Structure: icosahedral, helical, complex (tailed phages), pleomorphic. Baltimore classification I-VII based on genome → mRNA strategy: dsDNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, (+)ssRNA, (−)ssRNA, RNA-RT, DNA-RT. Giant viruses (Mimivirus) blur boundaries. Phages dominate the biosphere. Life cycles: attachment, entry, replication (cytoplasm or nucleus), assembly, release (lysis or budding); lytic vs lysogenic (lambda); latency (herpes neurons, HIV CD4 reservoir, HBV cccDNA). Reverse transcription Baltimore + Temin 1970 violated central dogma + drove HIV biology + cDNA toolkit. Major human viruses: HIV (Montagnier + Gallo Nobel 2008), influenza, HBV/HCV (DAAs), herpes, HPV (zur Hausen), Ebola, coronaviruses (SARS/MERS/SARS-CoV-2 mRNA vaccines Karikó + Weissman Nobel 2023), Zika. Phage therapy d'Hérelle 1917 + Eliava Institute Tbilisi; modern revival driven by AMR (Hatfull, Patterson). Concludes: virology is both an immediate medical priority + a foundation for tool-building across all of molecular biology.
